cf.title: Use-after-free of a shared Path in add_path()/add_partial_path()

input.subject: Use-after-free of a shared Path in add_path()/add_partial_path()

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The problem is stated with two reproducers, Richard Guo confirmed the bug on v19 and master in message #3, and the fix changes no signature or user-visible behaviour. The remaining points are the choice among the parent_rel check, a flat copy and reference counting, and the back-patch range, which a planner committer has to settle.

brief.title: Skip pfree() of a Path owned by another rel in add_path()
brief.problem: add_path() and add_partial_path() free dominated or rejected paths, assuming no other rel references them. grouping_planner() and create_ordered_paths() pass in paths that still belong to another rel, so a freed path can leave a Gather subpath dangling. Planning then fails with "ERROR: unrecognized node type: N" for some UNION queries with a set-returning function under parallel query.
brief.proposed_design: add_path() and add_partial_path() skip the pfree() when path->parent differs from parent_rel, next to the existing IndexPath exemption. The author relies on every create_*_path() constructor setting path->parent before the path reaches add_path(), so a mismatch marks a path borrowed from another rel. No caller changes; 0002 adds two regression tests to select_parallel.sql.
author_claims: The same defect shows up independently in grouping_planner() and create_ordered_paths(), so a general check beats fixing each call site.
The fix also covers the 2023 postgres_fdw report, which had no standalone reproducer.
The bug exists on all branches; the author first said v18 only and corrected this after Richard's v19 reproducer.
The fix is small and has no API impact, so it suits back-patching better than copying paths or reference counting.
The postgres_fdw leak it causes is a node or two per query, freed with the planning memory context.
brief.thread_state: Richard Guo reproduced the bug on v19 and master and thinks the parent_rel check works, while naming flat copy and reference counting as alternatives. Ashutosh Bapat points to an earlier discussion that found reference counting invasive; the author asks whether Richard will take the patch over, with no reply yet.
unclear: The material does not show that every create_*_path() constructor, including extension and FDW paths, sets path->parent to the rel it is added to.
The 2023 postgres_fdw case has no regression test, so only a manual debug elog shows that the fix covers it.
No reviewer has said how far back to back-patch; the CommitFest entry targets 18.
The thread does not say whether other paths share across rels with path->parent equal to parent_rel, which the check would miss.
Planner memory use with the leak has not been measured beyond the postgres_fdw estimate.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: add_path() and add_partial_path() keep their signatures, but FDW and custom paths whose parent differs from parent_rel are no longer freed.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: The patch changes when add_path() and add_partial_path() free a dominated or rejected path; plan choice is meant to stay the same.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The bug is on all branches and the author asks for a back-patch; no reviewer has said how far back.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The fix relies on every path constructor setting path->parent, a rule future path types must keep.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: add_path() runs for every candidate path; the patch adds one pointer compare and keeps some paths until planning ends.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which create_*_path() constructors, including FDW and custom scan paths, were checked to set path->parent to the rel later passed to add_path()?
Can a path be shared across rels while path->parent equals parent_rel, so that the check still frees it?
How far back should the fix go, and does Richard Guo's v19 reproducer also fail on the older supported branches?
Why is the parent_rel check preferred over a flat copy of the path at the two call sites, which Richard Guo says also fixes the bug?
How much extra planner memory do the unfreed paths cost on a query with many partitions or many postgres_fdw upper paths?

committability.owner_note: Needs a committer who knows the planner's path generation and upper-rel code. Richard Guo reviewed in message #3; the visible thread does not show whether he will commit it.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a back-patched change to add_path() memory rules on all supported branches, including extension paths that the regression suite does not cover, for the life of those branches.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted a v2 with a second regression test after review and asked whether Richard Guo will take the patch over, which suggests continued engagement.

priority.reason: This is a planner failure reachable from plain SQL under parallel query, reproduced by a reviewer on v19 and master. The patch is about 7 KiB in two planner files plus tests, with no API change.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody here could check that every path constructor sets path->parent as the fix assumes, or whether the patch updates the add_path() header comment and optimizer/README. The create_ordered_paths() case has no regression test, so its coverage rests on the author's manual check.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Consider incremental sort for fractional paths in generate_orderappend_paths
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch extends get_cheapest_fractional_path_for_pathkeys() so it can optionally add an incremental sort on top of partially sorted child paths when generate_orderedappend_paths() builds fractional paths for LIMIT queries. This is the follow-up to an already committed change that made generate_orderedappend_paths() consider fractional cheapest paths.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The PoC was incomplete: execution failed with a segfault in CheckVarSlotCompatibility, the patch failed tests for months, and building incremental sort paths only to discard most of them looked too expensive. After two months without progress, Andres Freund proposed returned with feedback, and the author agreed it needed much more work than the commitfest allowed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think it's a useful improvement, but it needs much more work
than is doable by the end of this CF.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix comment about generate_gather_paths
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch updates comments that still name generate_gather_paths() so they name generate_useful_gather_paths(), which the optimizer calls instead since commit ba3e76c. It changes comments only.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra found that the comment in create_ordered_paths() also describes what the function does, and that description no longer holds: generate_useful_gather_paths also builds paths with sorts, which are not order-preserving. That comment needed more rework. The author did not reply for more than a month, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
For example it says it generates order-preserving Gather Merge paths,
but generate_useful_gather_paths also generates paths with sorts (which
are clearly not order-preserving).

precedents_retrieved.title: Partial aggregates push down
precedents_retrieved.summary: postgres_fdw pushes partial aggregation to the remote server for aggregates marked safe by a new pg_aggregate flag (set for min/max/sum/count). For aggregates with internal state, a new converter function runs locally and turns the remote aggregate result into the local partial-aggregate state.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra was still not convinced of the approach in the last review. He saw no clear path to aggregates with complex states such as avg(), and he doubted that the aggpartialpushdownsafe flag without version checks ensures the remote node represents the state the same way. The author agreed he did not know how to handle complex states, and postgres_fdw has no way to learn the remote server version at planning time. The visible messages do not show further discussion before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
1) It's not clear to me how could this get extended to aggregates with
more complex aggregate states, to support e.g. avg() and similar fairly
common aggregates.

precedents_retrieved.title: Partial aggregates push down
precedents_retrieved.summary: Let postgres_fdw push partial aggregation down to remote servers, so each shard computes a partial aggregate state and the local server finalizes it. Early versions handled simple aggregates such as count, min, max and sum, and later versions extended this to aggregates with internal states, using added partial aggregate functions and a remote version check.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas said two major areas of work remained before the feature could be committed. Approach #2, which does the pushdown with an SQL keyword instead of separate partial aggregate functions for each aggregate, still needed investigation. Sending serialized bytea states between servers that cannot fully trust each other also needed design work and consensus. The entry closed as returned with feedback because, as vignesh C wrote, there was "still some work" left.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: In addition, the problems around transmitting serialized bytea blobs between machines that can't be assumed to fully trust each other will need to be addressed in some way, which seems like it will require a good deal of design work, forming some kind of consensus, and then implementation work to follow.

precedents_retrieved.title: Partial aggregates push down
precedents_retrieved.summary: Push partial aggregation down to remote servers through postgres_fdw, so each shard computes a partial aggregate state and the local server combines and finalizes the states. The first version allowed only simple aggregates such as count, max, min and sum, chosen by name, and later work tried to extend it to aggregates with an internal state type, such as avg.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages show no agreed method for sending partial states of aggregates with an internal state type, such as avg(bigint), avg(numeric) or avg(interval). The thread compared new export functions, new data types such as int128, and a record built from a list of type OIDs. Tomas Vondra said serial/deserial functions are not stable across releases. He also said that limiting pushdown to the same minor version would block it during node-by-node upgrades. The visible messages contain no closing message, and Bruce Momjian wrote that the docs were on hold until a transfer method was chosen.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: For serial/deserial we make no guarantees, it can change even in a minor release. But here we need something stable even for major releases, to allow pushdown when querying older server.

precedents_retrieved.title: partial heap only tuples
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds partial heap only tuples (PHOT), so an update creates new index tuples only for indexes whose columns changed, and those index tuples point to the new heap tuple. Index scans follow a PHOT chain only while their own indexed columns stay unchanged, and pruning of PHOT chains is restricted.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stopped applying to HEAD, and the entry was set to Waiting for Author in July 2021. No updated patch was posted, so the entry was returned with feedback in November 2021. The visible messages show design concerns, such as index create/drop handling and long-term heap fragmentation, but no objection that decided the outcome.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: As no update has been posted, the patch still doesn't apply.

precedents_retrieved.title: Optimize Numeric using fixed buffer reducing pallocs for small numbers
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a small fixed digit buffer to NumericVar, with a buf_len field, so that small numerics avoid palloc/pfree in numeric.c. Later versions reuse allocated buffers and change add_var(), div_var() and similar functions so the result may no longer be one of the operands.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Dean Rasheed found the change too invasive for gains of a few percent, with regressions in some cases such as generate_series() and a sqrt/sum series. He objected to low-level functions no longer accepting the result as an input, and proposed instead to reuse the digit buffer in make_result(); Joel Jacobson agreed to abandon the fixed buffer approach. No one pursued the alternative patch, and Peter Eisentraut returned the entry as inactive.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So IMO the results just don't justify such an extensive set of
changes, and I think we should abandon this fixed buffer approach.

precedents_retrieved.title: Optimizing Node Files Support
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changed gen_node_support.pl to make the generated node support files smaller and faster. It replaced runs of COPY_SCALAR_FIELD and COPY_LOCATION_FIELD calls with one memcpy, dropped NULL assignments already covered by palloc0, added first-element checks before memcmp and strcmp, and ignored unused pg_strtok results.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author offered no profiling or benchmarks to show a speed gain, and Tom Lane measured only a small drop in copyfuncs.o size. Tom Lane preferred to keep listing every field explicitly, to avoid errors of omission. John Naylor said one change added a multiple-evaluation hazard and others caused code churn or looked worse. The CFM closed it, asking for real performance gains that do not make the code harder to maintain.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think you're wasting people's time if you don't provide some performance measurements showing that this is worth doing from a speed standpoint.

precedents_retrieved.title: Don't shut down Gather[Merge] early under Limit.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Don't shut down Gather[Merge] early under Limit.
Reverted commit(s): Fix buffer usage stats for parallel nodes.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Revert part of commit 19df1702f5.

Early shutdown was added by that commit so that we could collect
statistics from workers, but unfortunately, it interacted badly with
rescans.  The problem is that we ended up destroying the parallel context
which is required for rescans.  This leads to rescans of a Limit node over
a Gather node to produce unpredictable results as it tries to access
destroyed parallel context.  By reverting the early shutdown code, we
might lose statistics in some cases of Limit over Gather [Merge], but that
will require further study to fix.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent records a reason that applies here. [P3] proposed an extension hook for the add_path() removal decision, a different idea with no recorded reason. Message #1 says the 2023 report stalled for lack of a reproducer, and this proposal adds two. Message #4 says reference counting was found invasive, which supports the smaller parent_rel check.

The patch adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object, dump content or psql change, and query results stay the same, so nothing touches the user-facing contract. The extension-visible effect, borrowed FDW paths no longer being freed, is an API and memory question for the design angle.

The patch changes only when the planner frees in-memory Path nodes during planning, so it adds no on-disk, WAL, catalog, wire-protocol or replication state. add_path() and add_partial_path() keep their signatures and no structs change, so back-patching raises no ABI concern from this angle.

The fix exposes nothing new to unprivileged users and adds no privilege, GUC or monitoring change. The skipped pfree() keeps a few extra Path nodes until the planning memory context is reset, which an unprivileged user cannot grow into a denial of service, and removing a use-after-free reachable from plain SQL helps security.

No objection from the maintenance angle: this is a crash fix that Richard Guo reproduced on v19 and master and supports (message #3), it changes no API, and it costs nothing on the hot path beyond one pointer compare in add_path(). The postgres_fdw leak is a node or two per query, freed with the planning context. Two points could not be checked without the code: whether every custom and FDW path sets path->parent consistently, and whether the patch updates the optimizer/README rule on freeing paths. [P3] is a hook proposal and does not apply here.

This is a bug fix for a planner use-after-free, so no existing feature or extension meets the need. The patch adds its check next to the existing IndexPath exemption in add_path() rather than building a second mechanism. [P3] proposed a path-removal hook, and the corpus records no reason for its outcome, so it does not apply here.

This is a bug fix for a planner use-after-free that a customer hit in production, a teammate reported independently, and a 2023 postgres_fdw report showed earlier. Richard Guo reproduced it on v19 and master (message #3), so demand is shown, and the benefit goes to every user of parallel query.
